analysis.one_liner: Funds housing and homelessness programs with new taxes on luxury property sales, anonymous buyers, and large landlords.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in five House committees for the rest of the 118th Congress and expired in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create new federal grants to house homeless and housing-unstable people, build permanently affordable housing, and stop cities from fining or arresting people for sleeping outside. To pay for it, it adds new taxes on very large real estate sales, property deals hidden behind anonymous shell companies, and big corporate landlords. It also adds grants to help homeless people vote and reforms federal homelessness programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeless and housing-unstable people, renters paying high shares of their income for housing, and low-income communities that would receive the new grants.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Community Development Block Grant Plus program for cities and states to build affordable housing and serve homeless, housing-unstable, and cost-burdened households [S2][S3].
Authorizes roughly $10 billion a year each for the Emergency Solutions Grant and Continuum of Care programs, $6 billion for CDBG Plus, and $1 billion for emergency food and shelter grants [S3].
Bars federal aid to governments that criminally punish homeless people for sleeping outside and requires procedures protecting homeless people's property under the 14th Amendment [S2][S3].
Funds pre-arrest diversion, mobile crisis teams, and alternatives to police responses to homelessness, with $100 million a year authorized [S3].
Provides grants so libraries serve homeless patrons, and requires that governments accepting funds protect homeless people's right to vote despite lacking a fixed address [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers and buyers of $10 million-plus properties, owners of property through anonymous entities, and large corporate landlords, who would pay the new taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Luxury property sellers and large landlords

drawbacks.text: The new taxes could raise costs in the housing market: the luxury transfer tax is split between buyer and seller, and the mass landlord rental tax applies to rent, which critics of such taxes say can be passed to tenants [S3].
The bill authorizes very large new federal spending — up to roughly $27 billion a year across its programs — which would add to the deficit if the dedicated tax revenues fall short [S3].

The mass landlord tax is waived for landlords in jurisdictions with rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protection laws, which gives those landlords an incentive to push for such local laws and adds administrative complexity [S3].
Requiring governments to stop enforcing bans on public camping as a condition of aid is contested: opponents of such policies argue it removes tools cities use to manage public spaces [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directs large, dedicated funding at homelessness and housing instability and ties the money to policies most homelessness researchers favor, while the costs fall mostly on very large property transactions and corporate landlords. The honest concerns are scale — tens of billions in new annual authorizations — and the risk that taxes on rent or transfers get passed through to tenants or buyers. It was a broad, ambitious bill with no Republican support and no path to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees when introduced, got a single subcommittee referral nearly two years later, and died when the 118th Congress ended without any committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 22, 2023 with 18 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Financial Services, House Administration, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means committees [S1][S5].
No committee took it up for more than a year and a half; on December 17, 2024, near the end of the Congress, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Work and Welfare [S5].
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a committee vote or floor vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords, luxury property owners, and users of anonymous property-buying entities are better off because the new taxes never became law; cities that enforce camping bans also avoid the funding conditions. Homeless and housing-unstable people gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large landlords and luxury property owners

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Housing Is a Human Right Act and gathered 29 cosponsors, all Democrats.

for.name: 29 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none of the support came from Republicans.

against.name: House committee chairs (Financial Services, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, House Administration)
against.role: Chairs of the five committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until it was referred to a subcommittee in the final weeks of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling the House floor and calendar in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats and there is no record of any Republican support; with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: A 1% tax on rent collected by landlords owning 1,000+ units in one metro area, 2,000+ units, or 500+ units across states, waived only in places with rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protections. Tenants in those buildings are the people paying the rent the tax touches.

industries.industry: Luxury real estate market (high-value property sellers and buyers)
industries.note: A 5% tax, split between buyer and seller, on real estate sales of $10 million or more. It affects only the top slice of property transactions and the revenue funds homeless programs.

A 10% tax on property sales involving entities whose true owners are not in public records, pushing real estate ownership toward transparency. These structures are used to shield ownership of high-value property.

industries.industry: Homeless services nonprofits and local housing providers
industries.note: The bill routes billions through existing HUD grant programs (Emergency Solutions, Continuum of Care) and new grants, expanding funding and contracts for service providers.
CDBG Plus funds can be used specifically to construct new affordable housing, acquire land, and convert hotels and other buildings, creating construction and rehabilitation work.
